questions.title: As an engineering lead, how do you roll out AI coding tools across a team?
questions.quick: I start with a small pilot, then expand with guardrails. I add repository instruction files describing conventions, commands and boundaries, set tool permissions so agents cannot run destructive commands or reach secrets, and agree what data may be sent to which tool. Review standards do not relax: AI-written code gets the same tests and human review. I track cycle time, review effort and escaped defects, not lines generated, and adjust training from what the data shows.
questions.revision: Pilot first; repo instruction files, restricted permissions, secret handling, unchanged review standards; measure cycle time and escaped defects, not lines generated.
questions.detailed:
Rollout is a **change-management and risk-control** exercise, not just licence purchasing.

## Phased plan

1. **Pilot** with a few volunteers across seniority levels on real work; collect friction and failure cases.
2. **Set policy:** approved tools, data classification rules, what may never be pasted or sent.
3. **Prepare repositories:** instruction files and working commands.
4. **Train** the wider team on prompting, verifying and failure modes.
5. **Expand** gradually and review metrics monthly.

## Guardrails

| Area | Practice |
|---|---|
| Repo instruction files | Document architecture, conventions, build and test commands, no-go areas; keep them in version control and review changes |
| Permissions | Read and edit by default; require approval for shell, network, deletes and pushes; sandbox where available |
| Secrets | Keep out of repos and prompts; use secret scanning, ignore files and environment isolation |
| Data terms | Check vendor data retention and training terms for the plan used; verify in current vendor documentation |
| Review | Same standards: tests, code review, security scanning; authors own what they merge |
| Auditability | Know who used which tool; keep logs where the tool supports it |

## Metrics

- **Cycle time** from start to merge, and review turnaround.
- **Escaped defects** and rework rate.
- Review effort per change and test coverage on AI-assisted changes.
- Developer satisfaction surveys.
- Avoid vanity measures such as lines or suggestions accepted.

## Common mistakes

- Mandating usage with no training or policy.
- Assuming productivity gains without measuring quality.
- Letting agents run with full shell and credentials.
- Juniors accepting output they cannot explain.
followUps: How would you handle a developer who pastes secrets into a prompt?
What would make you pause the rollout?
How do you keep instruction files current?

questions.title: How would you evaluate Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf and GitHub Copilot for your team?
questions.quick: I would run a structured trial rather than rely on demos or opinion. I pick representative tasks from our own backlog, such as a bug fix, a feature, a refactor and test writing, and have developers use each tool on comparable work. I compare review effort, defect rate, time to merge, security and data terms, admin controls and auditability, and cost. These tools change quickly, so I verify current features and terms, and I do not assume a single winner for every team.
questions.revision: Structured trial on representative tasks; compare review effort, defects, time to merge, data terms, auditability, admin controls and cost. No assumed winner; verify current terms.
questions.detailed:
These products differ in form (terminal agent, AI-first editor, editor extension) and change fast, so I evaluate **against our needs with evidence** and check current vendor documentation.

## Evaluation design

1. **Define criteria** and weights before trying anything.
2. **Choose representative tasks** from our own codebase: bug fix, small feature, cross-file refactor, test generation, unfamiliar-code explanation, a migration.
3. **Give each tool comparable tasks** and rotate developers to reduce bias.
4. **Measure** outcomes, not impressions.
5. **Review security and procurement** in parallel.

## Criteria

| Criterion | What to look at |
|---|---|
| Quality | Does the change work, pass tests and fit conventions? |
| Review effort | Time reviewers spend and size of corrections |
| Defect rate | Bugs found in review and after merge |
| Context handling | Behaviour on our large or legacy repositories |
| Workflow fit | IDE preference, terminal use, CI, pull request integration |
| Data terms | Retention, training use, regional options, plan differences |
| Controls | Permission modes, policy management, single sign-on, audit logs |
| Model choice | Which models are available and how they change |
| Cost | Seats plus usage, predictability |

## Scoring

Use a simple weighted matrix and record qualitative notes. Include a **reviewer's view** as well as the author's, since fast generation can hide slow review.

## Caveats

- Small trials are noisy; repeat tasks and avoid cherry-picking.
- Results shift with model updates, so schedule a re-evaluation.
- Teams may reasonably use more than one tool.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing from a vendor demo or social media.
- Testing only greenfield toy tasks.
- Ignoring data-handling terms until after adoption.
- Declaring a permanent winner.
followUps: Which criteria would you weight highest for a regulated team?
How do you reduce bias in a trial?

questions.title: What is a research spike, and how do you make it useful?
questions.quick: A spike is a time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty before committing to build. I start with a hypothesis or question, set a fixed time-box, and define success criteria in advance, such as latency under a target or a feasible integration path. The output is a decision, not a half-built feature: a short write-up with evidence, options, recommendation and risks. AI tools can speed experiments, but the conclusion still needs verified evidence.
questions.revision: A spike is a time-boxed investigation. State a hypothesis, fix the time-box, define success criteria, and end with a documented decision, not unfinished code.
questions.detailed:
A **research spike** answers a question that blocks planning, such as whether a library fits, whether an integration is feasible or whether a model meets a quality bar.

## Structure

| Element | Example (hypothetical) |
|---|---|
| Question or hypothesis | "A retrieval approach can answer 80 per cent of support questions from our documents" |
| Time-box | Two days; stop when it expires |
| Success criteria | Measured against a small labelled sample |
| Scope limits | Throwaway code; no production hardening |
| Output | A decision memo |

## Making it useful

1. **Write the question first.** Vague exploration expands to fill any time.
2. **Time-box strictly.** At the end, report what you know even if the answer is "unclear", with what would resolve it.
3. **Agree success and failure criteria beforehand** so results are not rationalised afterwards.
4. **Test the riskiest assumption first**, such as security, scale or data quality.
5. **Produce a decision:** options considered, evidence, recommendation, risks, estimate and next steps.
6. **Share it** with the team and keep it in the repository or wiki.
7. **Discard or isolate the code** so prototype shortcuts do not leak into production.

## Using AI in a spike

AI assistants can scaffold prototypes and summarise documentation quickly. Verify claims against primary documentation and real runs, and record what was checked.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a spike as the start of the feature and shipping the prototype.
- No time-box, so it runs for weeks.
- Reporting impressions with no data.
- Not recording negative results, which prevents the same spike being repeated.
followUps: What do you do if the time-box ends with no answer?
How is a spike different from a proof of concept?
How do you estimate work after a spike?

questions.title: How do you adopt spec-driven AI development methods such as BMAD or spec-kit style workflows without cargo-culting?
questions.quick: These methods share an idea: give AI agents structure through roles such as analyst, architect and developer, written specifications, small stories and acceptance criteria, so work is repeatable rather than ad hoc prompting. I would verify the specific project and its current version, then trial it on one real feature. I adopt only the parts that improve repeatability and quality, drop ceremony that adds no value, and keep human review of specs and code.
questions.revision: Shared idea: agent roles, specs, stories and acceptance criteria for repeatability. Verify the project and version, pilot on one feature, adopt only what measurably helps.
questions.detailed:
Methods in this family, including BMAD-style agent teams and spec-kit style workflows, **structure how people and AI agents move from idea to code**. I would **verify the specific project, its current version and documentation** before relying on any detail, since these evolve quickly.

## The general idea

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Agent roles (analyst, product owner, architect, developer, tester) | Separate concerns and prompts |
| Written specification | A durable source of truth the agent and humans share |
| Plan and tasks or stories | Small, reviewable units of work |
| Acceptance criteria | Testable definition of done |
| Checkpoints | Human review between stages |

The appeal is **repeatability**: the same inputs produce a more consistent process than ad hoc chat.

## Adopting without cargo-culting

1. **State the problem:** inconsistent output, rework from unclear requirements, or poor handover.
2. **Pilot on one real feature** with a small group; compare with the usual approach on cycle time, rework and defects.
3. **Adopt selectively.** Keep specs and acceptance criteria if they cut rework; drop role-play or documents nobody reads.
4. **Keep humans accountable:** review specs and diffs; an agent-written spec can be confidently wrong.
5. **Adapt to our context:** existing templates, definition of done, tooling and compliance needs.
6. **Review periodically** and retire steps that no longer help.

## Signals of cargo-culting

- Producing every document because the method lists it.
- Specs longer than the code they describe.
- Measuring adherence to the method rather than outcomes.
- Applying heavy process to a one-line fix.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a method as a guarantee of quality.
- Not testing against acceptance criteria.
- Letting specs drift from the code.
- Adopting a young project without checking maintenance and licence.
followUps: How would you decide the pilot succeeded?
How do you keep specs and code in sync?
